breath_title: Safe to struggle, safe to say so.
breath_text: A new 5-item scale offers a quick check on whether trainees feel safe sharing ideas, uncertainty, and mistakes. Residents who went through remediation echo it: transparency and personalization make or break the process. And as EHR metrics like TRACERs reveal each resident's practice patterns, how we share that data matters as much as the data.

coffee.title: Coffee break with Beth
coffee.note: In my own words. Written by Beth, not AI.
paragraphs: How fun to see colleagues at my institution doing great scholarship on standardized ILP Forms. I took a look at their template - I saw areas of overlap with what we ask in our program, and of course some new ideas. I was intrigued by their first question: Please describe your personal and professional core values.

Golly, that's a big one. It sent me into a bit of a spiral wondering if I can define my own core values. I landed on kindness, family, growth. Not sure how well I live these broad values but maybe I should have an ILP with myself once or twice a year to check in on how I'm doing.

top.headline: Psychological safety, measured in 5 questions
bullets: One health system put 9 candidate items in its annual trainee survey (400 of 480 answered) and trimmed them to 5: sharing ideas, giving and receiving feedback, expressing uncertainty, and mistakes as learning.
One factor, strong fit (CFI 0.99), omega 0.91, r = 0.67 with an external psych safety measure.
top.tip: short enough for an end-of-rotation survey, so you can trend it by site or team. Caveat: single-institution evidence.
top.citation: Tcheroyan R, Roberts MB, Joshi ART, et al. J Grad Med Educ. 2026;18(4):407-414. PMID 42602734. doi:10.4300/JGME-D-25-00666.1

top.headline: Remediation through residents' eyes: be transparent, make it personal
bullets: National qualitative study: 11 pediatric residents who had been through remediation (2024).
Themes: weak feedback systems, too little transparency and personalization, and a toll on well-being and careers. The authors updated their PD-based remediation model.
top.tip: residents want a transparent, personal process that feels psychologically safe. Pairs with last week's APPD "Trainee in Difficulty" piece.
top.citation: Cahaney C, Li ST, Nelsen E, et al. Acad Pediatr. Online June 18, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.acap.2026.103343

top.headline: TRACERs: your EHR may already know how each resident orders insulin
bullets: 3 IM programs built 2 automated, resident-attributed measures of inpatient diabetes care; EHR extraction matched expert review (96%+ sensitivity, 95%+ specificity).
In 615 residents and 6,192 admissions, discouraged bolus-only insulin ran 26.7%-42.6% by program, and residents varied more than programs.
top.tip: a preview of real-time, practice-based data for CCCs, with real barriers (different EHRs, tricky attribution).
top.citation: Burk-Rafel J, Sebok-Syer SS, Larson I, et al. Acad Med. Online July 28, 2026. doi:10.1093/acamed/wvag239

acadpeds.text: "Nothing You Can Say." A discussion piece. Title only; no abstract.
Med ed tracks pay off. Grads of one residency's medical education track (45/69 responded): 66% of attendings held formal educator roles; 89% said the track helped.
Immigrant families. 49% of 488 pediatricians felt prepared to care for children in immigrant families; bilingual staff (aOR 1.92) and care coordination (aOR 1.89) helped.
